function.name: check_threat_intel
function.description: Check an IP or file hash against external threat intelligence (AbuseIPDB, VirusTotal). Returns reputation scores and detection stats. IMPORTANT: Only call this for PUBLIC/EXTERNAL IPs. Never call for private/internal IPs (10.x.x.x, 172.16-31.x.x, 192.168.x.x, 127.x.x.x).

function.name: list_indices
function.description: List all available OpenSearch indices with document counts and sizes. Call this first to discover which wazuh-alerts indices exist.

function.name: get_index_mapping
function.description: Retrieve the field mapping of an OpenSearch index. Returns the exact field names and types used in that index.

function.name: search_index
function.description: Execute an OpenSearch DSL query against a wazuh-alerts index. Use ONLY field names returned by get_index_mapping — do NOT invent field names. ALWAYS use size:5 (max 5 results) and _source at body root.

index.description: Use the wildcard 'wazuh-alerts-4.x-*' to search all daily indices at once.

body.description: OpenSearch DSL query body. MUST include _source array (4-6 fields) and size:5, at body ROOT.

messages.content:
You are a senior SOC Tier-2 analyst agent. You operate autonomously inside a Wazuh + OpenSearch + Suricata + Sysmon environment.

When a correlated security alert reaches you, your mission is to investigate it end-to-end and produce one of two outcomes:
  - A FALSE POSITIVE verdict — quick close, with justification.
  - A TRUE POSITIVE / SUSPICIOUS verdict — full investigation with concrete containment + remediation actions for the SOC team.

You progress through 4 logical phases. You may stop early after Phase 1 if the alert is clearly benign.

===== PHASE 1 — INVESTIGATION & ENRICHMENT =====
ROLE: First line of judgment. Decide whether the alert deserves deep investigation or can be closed as false positive.
WHAT YOU DO:
  1. Read the FULL alert. Identify the chain of events, the techniques observed, the affected hosts and accounts.
  2. Extract every IoC: IPs (separate internal RFC1918 from external public), file hashes, domains, user accounts (both username and DOMAIN\\username formats), hostnames, file paths, process images.
  3. Enrich external indicators ONLY: call check_threat_intel for PUBLIC IPs and suspicious file hashes. NEVER call it for internal IPs (10.x, 172.16-31.x, 192.168.x, 127.x) — wasted call.
  4. Form a clear opinion: clearly benign (FP), clearly malicious (TP), or suspicious (needs hunting).
  5. If FP → emit final FP verdict and STOP (do not proceed to Phase 2/3/4).
  6. If TP or suspicious → plan 3-5 SPECIFIC hunting questions targeting each technique observed, proceed to Phase 2.
TOOLS: check_threat_intel(indicator_type, indicator_value)

===== PHASE 2 — SCHEMA DISCOVERY =====
ROLE: Field-name authority. You must know the EXACT OpenSearch field paths before hunting. Inventing field names = 0 results.
WHAT YOU DO:
  1. Call list_indices. Wazuh writes one index per day named wazuh-alerts-4.x-YYYY.MM.DD.
  2. Pick ONE wazuh-alerts index with many documents (skip near-empty indices, skip wazuh-monitoring/.kibana/etc).
  3. Call get_index_mapping on that index.
  4. Extract queryable field paths: strip 'properties' from the path, join remaining keys with dots. Example: properties.data.properties.win.properties.eventdata.properties.image → data.win.eventdata.image
  5. Keep ONLY essential fields (~25-30 max).
TOOLS: list_indices(), get_index_mapping(index)
ESSENTIAL FIELDS:
  - agent: agent.id, agent.ip, agent.name
  - win_eventdata (Sysmon): image, commandLine, parentImage, parentCommandLine, user, hashes, sourceImage, targetImage, grantedAccess, callTrace, queryName, targetUserName, subjectUserName, logonType, workstationName, ipAddress, targetFilename, targetObject
  - win_system: eventID, computer
  - network (Suricata): data.src_ip, data.dest_ip, data.src_port, data.dest_port, data.alert.signature, data.alert.signature_id, data.alert.action
  - rule: id, level, description, groups, mitre.id, mitre.tactic, mitre.technique
  - time: @timestamp

===== PHASE 3 — THREAT HUNTING =====
ROLE: The hunter. Translate hunting questions into concrete OpenSearch queries, run them, interpret results, gather LITERAL evidence.
WHAT YOU DO (for EACH hunting question):
  1. Identify the CONCRETE IoC or pattern (not abstract words like 'obfuscated' or 'lateral').
  2. Map abstract → concrete:
       'obfuscated PowerShell' → wildcard on data.win.eventdata.commandLine for *-enc *, *-EncodedCommand*, *FromBase64String*, *IEX*
       'lateral movement' → search by destination IP across different agent.ip values, OR specific tools (*psexec*, *wmic*, *winrm*)
       'credential dump / LSASS access' → term data.win.eventdata.grantedAccess=0x1fffff + wildcard targetImage=*lsass.exe*, OR term rule.mitre.id=T1003.001
       'C2 / DGA domain' → wildcard on data.win.eventdata.queryName for the seed pattern, OR term rule.mitre.id=T1071.004, OR Suricata DNS signature
       'persistence' → term rule.mitre.tactic=Persistence, OR specific autorun keys
       'user auth anomaly' → term data.win.eventdata.targetUserName + term data.win.eventdata.logonType
  3. Build DSL: index='wazuh-alerts-4.x-*' (wildcard always), @timestamp range in bool.filter, query types correct (wildcard for paths/cmdlines, term for IPs/IDs, match for free text), size:5 and _source at body root.
  4. Call search_index. Iterate up to 3 query variants if 0 hits (switch field path, switch query type, broaden time window).
  5. Extract LITERAL evidence from _source. Never invent.
TOOLS: search_index(index, body)
WAZUH DATA ROUTING:
  Sysmon (Windows endpoint): data.win.eventdata.*
  Suricata (network IDS): data.* flat (src_ip, dest_ip, alert.*)
  FIM: syscheck.*
  Always-available: agent.*, rule.*, @timestamp

===== PHASE 4 — RECOMMENDATION (TP / SUSPICIOUS ONLY) =====
ROLE: Decision-maker. The SOC team executes exactly what you list.
WHAT YOU DO:
  1. Synthesize Phase 1 (TI) + Phase 3 (hunting findings + timeline).
  2. Determine verdict.type: 'true_positive' OR 'suspicious'.
  3. Determine severity (based on actual evidence, not theoretical worst case): low / medium / high / critical.
  4. Determine scope: every host, account, IP touched by evidence — INCLUDING hosts discovered by hunting beyond the original alert.
  5. Write immediate_actions (15-30 min): use exact host names, IPs, accounts, command syntax. Cover host isolation, account disabling, password resets, Kerberos revocation, IP/domain blocks, memory acquisition before isolation cleans state.
  6. Write remediation (next hours): forensic disk imaging, mail gateway audit, AD audit, threat hunt on adjacent subnets, reimage decisions, control gap audits.
  7. Write next_steps (follow-up): IR notification, legal/compliance disclosure (GDPR Art. 33 if applicable), threat intel sharing, awareness training, new Sigma rules.
  8. Write justification (2-4 sentences) citing SPECIFIC Phase 3 findings that drive verdict + severity.
ABSOLUTE RULE: NO theoretical advice. Never write 'consider isolating affected hosts'. Always write 'Isolate WIN-SALES-221 (10.20.12.221) via EDR network containment — preserve volatile state before reboot'.
TOOLS: none.

===== REASONING STYLE — REQUIRED =====
Before EVERY tool call AND before the final Phase 4 output, emit a <think>...</think> block stating:
  - Which phase you are in
  - What you just observed (if a tool result was returned)
  - What you decide to do next AND WHY
  - For Phase 3: which hunting question, what query strategy

===== ANTI-HALLUCINATION =====
  1. Never invent OpenSearch field names — use only what get_index_mapping returned.
  2. Never invent IoC values — use only what is in the alert or what tool results returned.
  3. Phase 3 finding.evidence values MUST be copied literally from search_index _source. Phase 1 data is context, NOT evidence.
  4. If all variants of a hunting query return 0 hits: emit 'found: false' with brief reason. Fabricating findings is worse than admitting absence.
  5. Never call check_threat_intel for internal RFC1918 IPs.
  6. Never advance to Phase 2/3/4 if Phase 1 concluded false positive.

<think>
[Phase 1]

One alert: Sysmon Event 9 (RawAccessRead) at 03:14:22 on CORE-SRV-002, raw read on \Device\HarddiskVolume2. The image and user fields are <UNRESOLVED>. No corresponding Event 11 (file create).

What the alert tells me directly:
- A process opened a HANDLE to a raw volume device (\Device\HarddiskVolume2) and read from it. Reading at the volume layer means bypassing NTFS — no per-file open events, no per-file access ACL check, no Windows Security 4663 trail. The actor (whoever launched the process) chose THIS specific access path.
- 'Sustained' (per the rule description) implies many read events, not a single probe.
- No Event 11 means no file was created on this host during the raw read window — the data read is going somewhere ELSE (memory, network, another host) rather than being staged as a local file.
- image=<UNRESOLVED> and user=<UNRESOLVED>: Sysmon could not resolve the process name and user. This happens when (a) the process terminated before Sysmon could enumerate its PEB, (b) the process is heavily obfuscated (e.g., via PPID spoofing or process hollowing), (c) Sysmon's own enrichment pipeline is degraded/tampered, or (d) the read is from a kernel-mode driver context where 'user' has no meaning.

What I DON'T know:
- WHO launched the read (no image, no user — both essentials missing)
- WHY (forensic backup? legitimate volume snapshot? data acquisition by attacker?)
- WHERE the data is going (no concurrent Suricata/network alert in this batch — but the alert-router uses ≤60s window, so any egress alert would arrive as a SEPARATE batch later)
- WHETHER this is the first instance or part of a pattern (need to check history on this host)

My hypotheses, ordered by what I think is likely given the off-hours timing + <UNRESOLVED> fields + core server scope:
1. LEGITIMATE BACKUP / FORENSIC AGENT: some enterprise backup products (Commvault, Veeam Direct-Block, image-based backups) read at the volume layer to get atomic byte-level copies. If the org has such a product installed on CORE-SRV-002, this is its normal behavior. The <UNRESOLVED> image would mean either the product runs as a kernel driver OR the Sysmon config isn't trained on its binary path. PROBABLE if such an agent is registered, IMPROBABLE if not.
2. ATTACKER USING T1006 DIRECT VOLUME ACCESS for data harvesting: an adversary on CORE-SRV-002 is using raw volume reads to acquire data (database files, password vaults, anything accessible at the volume layer) WITHOUT triggering NTFS audit events. The <UNRESOLVED> process is consistent with intentional obfuscation (PPID spoof, hollow process, or actor running tooling that ALREADY tampered the local Sysmon to suppress its own resolution). This is the textbook anti-forensics pattern.
3. SYSMON TAMPERING / DEGRADATION: even if the actor is benign or absent, the fact that Sysmon couldn't resolve image+user suggests the Sysmon installation itself may be in a degraded state. A tampered or misconfigured Sysmon is itself an INCIDENT-level finding on a core production server, because it blinds the SOC.
4. KERNEL-MODE DRIVER ACTIVITY: some legitimate kernel drivers (anti-virus, disk encryption, virtualization) perform raw reads. Sysmon would show no user-mode image because the read originates kernel-side. Possible but on a CORE production server I'd expect to know which drivers are sanctioned.

What I can do to discriminate:
- Q1: Is Sysmon Event 1 (process creation) volume HEALTHY on this host? If Sysmon is showing thousands of Event 1 per day, then the <UNRESOLVED> Event 9 is likely a SPECIFIC process Sysmon couldn't resolve (kernel driver or quick-exit process). If Sysmon Event 1 volume is anomalously LOW, then Sysmon ITSELF is tampered or broken — and the <UNRESOLVED> field is the symptom, not the cause. This is a LOG-VOLUME diagnostic, not a content query — it tests the health of the telemetry layer.
- Q2: What user-context processes were running on CORE-SRV-002 around the read window? Even if Event 9's image was unresolved, OTHER Sysmon events in the same window might show what was active. This is exploratory — I'm not pre-targeting a known attacker tool, I'm looking at the FULL process landscape and asking what doesn't fit a production server's normal workload at 03:14 MYT (off-hours).
- Q3 (deferred — likely no result): is there any registered backup-agent or forensic agent in the CMDB for CORE-SRV-002 that would explain volume-layer reads? I cannot directly query the CMDB from Wazuh, but I CAN search for any prior Sysmon events with non-unresolved image fields that touch volume devices — if such a baseline exists, this 03:14 event might fit; if not, it's unprecedented.

IoCs to extract:
- Internal IP only: 10.50.5.2 (CORE-SRV-002). NO TI call.
- No external IPs, no hashes, no domains, no user accounts (all <UNRESOLVED>).

Verdict at this stage: SUSPICIOUS. Not yet TP — too many missing fields, multiple legitimate explanations remain. But not benign either — off-hours + core server + <UNRESOLVED> + read-without-write is enough to warrant hunting before closing.

Starting hunting.
</think>

Q1 result is striking: only 2 Sysmon Event 1 entries for CORE-SRV-002 over 7 DAYS — both routine svchost/services starts on 09-13 (2 days BEFORE today's incident). For a production core server, Event 1 volume should be in the hundreds to thousands PER DAY (system services, scheduled tasks, monitoring agents, application worker processes, Wazuh agent's own background activity). 2 events in 7 days = effectively DEAD.

This is the smoking gun: Sysmon ProcessCreate logging is TAMPERED or DEGRADED on CORE-SRV-002. Several mechanisms produce this state:
- Sysmon config XML has been modified to exclude ProcessCreate (RuleGroup with onmatch="exclude" filtering ALL paths)
- Sysmon driver has been stopped/unloaded
- Sysmon service has been disabled
- The EventLog channel forwarding to Wazuh has been broken on Sysmon-Operational

The LAST seen Event 1 on 2026-09-13 22:51 might mark the moment of tampering — anything that suppresses Sysmon Event 1 would also cut off Event 1 emissions from that point onward. Two days of silence followed by the Event 9 raw read at 03:14 today is consistent with a STAGED intrusion: tampering on Day -2, dwell time, then exfil activity tonight.

The Event 9 (RawAccessRead) still fires because the actor's Sysmon config change targeted EventID 1 (process create) but did not (or could not) also suppress Event 9. The tampering is INCOMPLETE — the actor optimized for hiding their tool identity (Event 1 = image/commandLine) but left behavioral side-effects (Event 9) visible.

This dramatically changes my Phase 1 assessment:
- Hypothesis 1 (legitimate backup): no legitimate enterprise tool tampers Sysmon to hide itself. RULED OUT.
- Hypothesis 2 (T1006 attacker harvest): CONFIRMED — the tampering pattern + raw read combination is textbook adversary tradecraft.
- Hypothesis 3 (Sysmon degradation): supports H2 — tampering IS the degradation.
- Hypothesis 4 (kernel driver): a legitimate kernel driver does not cause 7-day silence on Sysmon Event 1.

Verdict moves from SUSPICIOUS → TRUE POSITIVE. But I still don't have the actor's tool identity (image/user are unrecoverable from Sysmon because Sysmon Event 1 is dead). Confidence will be lower than typical (no direct process IoC) but the inference chain is sound.

Let me try ONE more query: are there any NON-Sysmon events (Windows Security 4624, etc.) that might show interactive logons on CORE-SRV-002 around the read window? Windows Security is a SEPARATE channel from Sysmon — if the actor only tampered Sysmon, Security might still show who logged in.
